questions.scenario: You want less sodium in one cup of soup. A has 300 mg per half-cup; B has 450 mg per cup. Which has less sodium for your one-cup portion?

options.text: A: 300 mg
B: 450 mg
They are equal

questions.explanation: Compare the amount you actually eat: one cup of A contains 600 mg, versus 450 mg in B. Label values depend on serving size.

questions.scenario: Two crackers have the same serving size. A has 4% Daily Value for sodium; B has 22%. Using FDA label guidance, which statement is accurate?

options.text: Both are low in sodium
A is low; B is high
Percent Daily Value cannot compare foods

questions.explanation: FDA treats 5% Daily Value or less per serving as low and 20% or more as high. This compares sodium, not every aspect of the foods.

questions.scenario: A yogurt label says Total Sugars 12 g, including 5 g Added Sugars. How much total sugar is in one serving?

options.text: 5 g

questions.explanation: Added sugars are part of total sugars, so do not add them again. The total is 12 g; 5 g of that is added sugar.

questions.scenario: A cereal label lists a serving of three-quarters of a cup. Does that tell every person how much cereal they should eat?

options.text: Yes, it is a personalized recommendation
No, it describes the label quantity and typical consumption
Yes, eating more always causes illness

questions.explanation: Label serving sizes describe amounts people typically consume, not a personal eating prescription. Use the amount you eat when reading nutrient values.

questions.scenario: A generally healthy adult walks briskly for 150 minutes a week. Which missing element would match CDC adult activity guidance?

options.text: Muscle-strengthening work for all major muscle groups on at least two days

questions.explanation: Adult guidance combines aerobic activity with muscle strengthening on two or more days. These are general guidelines; adapt activities to your abilities.

questions.scenario: You are preparing raw chicken and a ready-to-eat salad. Which is the safer method?

options.text: Rinse the chicken over the salad bowl
Use separate boards, keep raw juices away, and check chicken reaches 165 degrees F with a thermometer
Reuse the raw-chicken board without washing

questions.explanation: Raw chicken can spread germs to salad. CDC recommends separation and a thermometer check at 165 degrees F (about 74 degrees C); washing raw chicken is unnecessary.

questions.scenario: Restaurant leftovers were refrigerated promptly and have stayed cold for five days. What matches CDC guidance?

options.text: Taste them to decide
Keep them for another week
Discard them

questions.explanation: CDC recommends eating refrigerated restaurant leftovers within three to four days and discarding them after that. A five-day-old portion is beyond that window.
